About this citation

A literary work in which Zarathustra is a speaker, not Nietzsche. The archive's locator names the part and the discourse ('On the Three Metamorphoses'), which is how the book refers to itself, because it has no chapter numbers.

Exact wording

English (as recorded here)
“Man is something that shall be overcome.”
German
“Der Mensch ist etwas, das überwunden werden soll.”

“Man is something that shall be overcome.” From Zarathustra's prologue; the verb is sollen, a requirement, not a prediction.

Forms in circulation that differ

  • “Man is something that shall be overcome.”
  • “Man is something to be surpassed.”

Attribution notes

Nietzsche, Also sprach Zarathustra, Prologue §3. The speaker is Zarathustra addressing the marketplace crowd about the Übermensch; quoting it as Nietzsche's bare definition of humanity without that frame turns a prophetic demand into a slogan about self-improvement.

What a locator tells you, and what it does not · How this archive traces a quotation

About Friedrich Nietzsche

Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German classical philologist who became a radical critic of morality, metaphysics, and modern culture. Appointed professor at Basel at twenty-four, he resigned from ill health and wrote in solitude across Switzerland, Italy, and Germany.

Interpretation

Zarathustra's declaration is about the human as a thing to be surpassed, not improved. The German verb implies going over and beyond, so the claim is that the human condition is a condition to be left behind. What follows in the book is the figure of the overman as whatever comes after, defined by self-creation rather than by any fixed nature. The sentence is provocative because it refuses to treat human nature as a standard.

Why it matters

It raises a question worth asking without the mythology: are you trying to become a better instance of what you already are, or something you cannot yet describe? The two produce very different plans.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “Man is something that shall be overcome.”?

“Man is something that shall be overcome.” comes from Also sprach Zarathustra, Prologue (1883–1885), attributed to Friedrich Nietzsche.

What does Friedrich Nietzsche mean by self?

To ask about the self is to ask what persists through experience, what can be known from the first-person point of view, and how character is formed. Some traditions treat the self as a substantial soul; others as a stream of experience, a social role, or a practical center of agency. This passage enters that discussion through self.

Is the wording of this Friedrich Nietzsche quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Man is something that shall be overcome.” Forms in circulation that differ: Man is something that shall be overcome. / Man is something to be surpassed. The German reads “Der Mensch ist etwas, das überwunden werden soll.”

Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Nietzsche, Also sprach Zarathustra, Prologue §3. The speaker is Zarathustra addressing the marketplace crowd about the Übermensch; quoting it as Nietzsche's bare definition of humanity without that frame turns a prophetic demand into a slogan about self-improvement.
